items.title: Min Aung Hlaing wins parliamentary vote to become Myanmar president

featured_image.name: Myanmar's General Min Aung Hlaing set to become president - Yahoo

items.description:
Myanmar's former military chief Min Aung Hlaing was elected president on Friday by the country's junta-installed parliament, completing a transition five years in the making from coup leader to nominal civilian head of state. The 69-year-old general, who seized power in 2021 by ousting the democratically elected government of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, won the presidency in a bicameral vote that was widely seen as a foregone conclusion, with pro-military lawmakers controlling roughly 86 percent of parliamentary seats.[1][2]

The vote, held at 10:00 a.m. local time in the capital Naypyidaw, saw members of both legislative chambers choose from among three vice-presidential candidates: Min Aung Hlaing, Nan Ni Ni Aye of the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party, and former Prime Minister U Nyo Saw, a retired lieutenant general and close Min Aung Hlaing ally. Union Parliament Speaker U Aung Lin Dwe had confirmed on Thursday that all three candidates met the constitutional qualifications for the presidency.[3][4][5][6]

items.title: U.S. Embassy urges Americans to leave Lebanon over Iran university threats

featured_image.name: Iran threatens US, Israel-linked universities across Middle East

items.description:
The U.S. Embassy in Beirut issued an urgent security alert on Friday urging all American citizens to depart Lebanon while commercial flights remain available, warning that Iran and its allied militias "may intend to target universities in Lebanon."[1][2]

The advisory described the security environment as "volatile and unpredictable," citing ongoing airstrikes, drone activity, and rocket fire across the country, particularly in southern Lebanon, the Beqaa region, and parts of Beirut. "Iran has specifically threatened American universities across the Middle East," the embassy said, though it did not identify any specific institutions at risk.[2][3][4]

items.description: Just over a month into the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, the economic fallout is rippling far beyond the Middle East, battering energy-dependent economies in Asia and straining European fiscal frameworks. items.title: U.S. jet shot down over Iran as bridge strike death toll rises to 13

featured_image.name: US F-15E fighter jet shot down over Iran

items.description:
A U.S. airstrike on Thursday destroyed the B1 bridge in Iran's Alborz province, a 136-meter structure that was the tallest bridge in the Middle East, killing at least eight people and wounding 95 others, according to Iranian officials. The death toll later climbed to 13 by Friday, Iranian state media reported.[1][2][3][4][5]

The strike marks a sharp escalation in the targeting of Iranian civilian infrastructure as Operation Epic Fury, which began on February 28, enters its fifth week.[6][7]

items.title: Iran drone strike on Riyadh embassy far worse than disclosed

featured_image.name: Iran targets U.S. allies, hits American Embassy in Riyadh - Axios

items.description: The March 3 Iranian drone strike on the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, caused far more destruction than the American and Saudi governments publicly acknowledged, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing current and former U.S. officials. Multiple floors of the embassy were heavily damaged, parts of the building remain "unrecoverable," and a fire sparked by the attack burned for twelve hours — a stark contrast to the Saudi Defense Ministry's initial assessment of "limited fire and minor material damage".[1][2][3]

items.title: Gaza Christians mark Good Friday as ceasefire strains

featured_image.name: Christian faithful gather in Gaza City to mark Good Friday

items.description:
Gaza City’s Christian community gathered at the Holy Family Church on Friday to mark Good Friday, a subdued observance that came as the enclave’s ceasefire with Israel remained in place but under strain. The service followed Palm Sunday celebrations at the same church less than a week earlier, one of the clearest signs that Holy Week rites have resumed in Gaza after long disruption from war.[1][2][3][4][5]

The prayers unfolded against a backdrop of continuing insecurity. Reuters reported on March 31 that Gaza health officials said Israeli fire had killed at least 700 people since the ceasefire took hold, while the Associated Press has described the truce as tenuous and marked by near-daily violence. That has left Gaza’s remaining Christians celebrating Easter season with caution rather than relief.[2][6][4][5]
